speaker: Steve Temple
title: Advanced Debugging
description:
Debugging has taken a bit of a bashing on the internet recently,  but I think it's a developer superpower. Allowing you to easily see what your code is doing and quickly find bugs that weren't obvious from looking through your code.

Most developers aren't fully utilising the tools available in Visual Studio and who has got time to really dive in and figure everything you could be doing. I'll save you that time but running through a lot of the available tools from the basic debugging to debugging complex applications. Moving into some of the tricky debugging scenarios such as remote debugging production servers and stepping into third party code.

A talk for those new to programming all the way up to experienced developers.

speaker: Kevin Smith
title: Fixing Broken Messaging: Pitfalls, Failures, and Solutions
description:
Messaging is a fundamental part of distributed systems, but poor messaging practices can lead to performance bottlenecks, increased coupling, and system failures.

In this session, we’ll explore the most common messaging pitfalls—such as excessive locking in handlers, oversized event payloads, improper deduplication strategies, and over-reliance on request-response messaging.

We’ll break down how these issues impact system scalability and reliability, and more importantly, how to avoid them. Expect to see some examples using .NET and MassTransit, and insights into building resilient, event-driven architectures.

Whether you're new to messaging or looking to refine your patterns, this talk will help you design messaging workflows that are scalable, maintainable, and efficient.

speaker: Aaron Green
title: How to have conversations which improve your teams, your life, and maybe even the world
description:
I believe we’re living through a breakdown in communication. As polarization grows, it’s become all too easy to dismiss those who disagree with us as ignorant, stupid, or even evil. Social media and echo chambers amplify this divide, but history shows us where this road can lead—like Athens in the Peloponnesian War, where populism and mistrust fractured a thriving society.

In this talk, I’ll explore how we got here, how assumptions and biases shape our interactions, and how we can start to bridge the divide. By understanding the dynamics of connection, listening with curiosity, and challenging our echo chambers, we can foster better conversations—ones that lead to stronger teams, healthier workplaces, and richer relationships.

These ideas have changed how I work, how I live, and how I connect with people. My hope is that they can do the same for you. Together, we can build better dialogues that improve our lives and maybe, in some small way, the world.

speaker: Jacqui Read
title: Surviving Complexity Through Software Design
description:
There has never been more pressure on software developers. Dealing with multiple tech stacks, devops pipelines, observability, and more. Add to that the pressure to deliver working software quickly and regularly and we end up with software that doesn't meet expectations and cannot be easily changed. But with so much else on their minds, when do teams think about design and architecture?

At The Ministry of Software Design we have been looking at how teams can incrementally own their design, and own their architecture, despite the complexity they are working with. Join this session to see how you can manage the complexity of your software design to create software that is evolvable and meets both user and business needs.

speaker: James Gaisford
title: Building with Integrity: Embracing Ethical Web Development
description:
The Dark Web. Crypto. Twitter. The web has evolved significantly since Tim Berners-Lee's original vision of a free and open web that connects us all. Over time, it has become clear that the web can be used in ways that subvert its original mission or even cause harm.

In this talk, we will explore the W3C's recently released Ethical Web Principles statement. You will be reminded of what the web should be and how we can build our applications in line with these principles. As developers and technologists, it's crucial to consider the consequences of our work as we continue to advance the web. By the end of this talk, you'll be reminded of the web's true potential and leave with some clear actions to help you shape a more ethical web.

speaker: Steven Read
title: Modern Software Architecture Review Best Practices
description:
Software Architecture reviews is a topic that rarely gets discussed at conferences, and equally rarely covered in books and blog posts. Writing and presenting your first review is a rite of passage for an architect; you never know when you may be in a situation where one is needed.

In this talk you will see how a modern architecture review is performed. We aren't talking about word documents that will never again see the light of day, we are talking about creating reusable knowledge management artefacts that the team will build on going forward. Think of it as a spring clean for software architecture.

Don't think you'll ever need to complete one? They are a useful exercise while on-boarding in a new team and learning a new product.

Have you run a well-architected framework review? You will be surprised at the differences.

speaker: Nurhak Kaya
title: Practical Guide to Unlocking Accessibility of Websites
description: In this hands-on session, we’ll dive into using powerful tools like WAVE to identify and address accessibility issues on your website. Learn how to use these tools to spot common barriers, from missing alt text to improper heading structure, and take actionable steps to improve your site’s accessibility. We’ll cover the basics of accessibility testing, how to interpret WAVE reports, and prioritize fixes to make sure your website is inclusive for all users. Whether you’re just starting out or looking to streamline your accessibility workflow, this session will provide practical guidance you can apply right away.

speaker: George Bell
title: What I learnt by attending a Hackathon and mentoring instead of writing code
description: Last year, I attended the NASA Space Apps Challenge here in Bristol. But rather than coding, I was there with a local charity called DigiLocal that helps marginalised young people develop digital skills. I spent the weekend mentoring a team of young people as they worked on their submission. This lightning talk will go over the things you learn by mentoring at a Hackathon, the challenges you face and the reasons why you should consider it.

speaker: Scott James
title: AzDO YAML Pipelines; bits and bobs
description: A short hodgepodge of what the UKHO is up to and tips & tricks on building pipelines.

speaker: Danielle Dias
title: Enhance Your Security Posture with the Power of Threat Modelling
description:
In the ever-evolving landscape of cybersecurity, securing your applications is a critical challenge. Attackers are constantly finding new ways to exploit vulnerabilities, highlighting the need for a proactive "shift-left" strategy to prevent threats from happening - even before a single line of code is written. Understanding and managing security early is essential, and that’s where Threat Modelling comes in.

This lightning talk will cover how Threat Modelling can transform your approach to security. You’ll learn what it is, why prioritising it is vital, and how to put it into practice effectively. You’ll see how this proactive method not only prevents threats but also reshapes your ability to stay ahead in a constantly changing threat landscape.

speaker: Anita Squires
title: Hidden voices/lost ideas
description:
If you ask most people to name a famous person associated with the internet they will probably say Tim Berners-Lee. He did create the World Wide Web, but without the work of Radia Perlman, Elizabeth Fienler and Karen Spark-Jones, it would not be half as useful to the everyday person. Let my talk introduce you to 10 women who helped shape the technology we use today and explain why not forgetting them can help us find more hidden voices in our day-to-day lives and use their ideas to move us forward.
For the past forty years, fewer women have enrolled in technology courses. Several articles pinpoint 1984 as the year that enrolment dropped off in steep decline. There were several factors to this drop off, including just a general view that women did not belong in the field, with Stephen Levy labelling them “horribly inefficient and wasteful things” in his book Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution.

speaker: Roger Barreto
title: Unleashing the Power of AI with Semantic Kernel: A Beginner-to-Intermediate Hands-On Guide
description:
Abstract:
Join this engaging and practical session designed to take participants on a journey from the foundational concepts of Semantic Kernel to its cutting-edge applications. We’ll start with the basics—core components and principles—and dive deeper as we code together. You’ll gain hands-on experience exploring exciting topics such as Small Language Models, Local Models, Plugins, AI Safety, Prompt Templating, and Multi-Modality. Discover how Semantic Kernel enables seamless integration of functionalities like chat completion, image and audio generation, and even executing local code with AI models.

This session will also showcase how to leverage OpenAPI to extend the power of Semantic Kernel, simplifying complex tasks while maintaining robust AI safety and performance. Whether you're a beginner or looking to deepen your understanding, this talk will equip you with practical insights and actionable skills for using Semantic Kernel in innovative ways.

speaker: Joe Glombek
title: Why am I being such a git about best practices?

speakerTaglines.joe-glombek: Senior .NET developer and lover of adventure

description: Are your git repos a dumping ground for code? I'm really fussy about how people use git - and that's a good thing. We'll take a look at branching strategies, the importance of commit messages and how often should you commit, anyway? Let's investigate how, with 5 simple tips, we can turn a code dump into a glorious archive of software and how this can save time, frustration and money.

speaker: John Kilmister
title: A Developers Guide to Getting the Most out of Containers
description:
Containers seem to be everywhere however are we getting the most out of them during the development lifecycle?

In this session, we will cover container basics before looking at the best practices for creating and tagging containers, examine how we can use dev containers to enhance our workflow, and examine test containers.

speaker: Carly Richmond
title: How to Destroy a DevOps Engineer
description:
Abstract

Retaining Software Developers is a significant challenge for teams. According to the Infragistics Reveal Survey, 37.5% of respondents expected difficulty in finding developers in 2023. To retain talent, it's essential to understand factors that lead to dissatisfaction.

Join me as I discuss antipatterns in management, development, testing and monitoring patterns that can stop you retaining awesome DevOps engineers.

Outline

I’ll cover:

- Alert volume evaluation, and how we alert bombardment leads to burnout and alert fatigue. I’ll also cover best practices for on-call rotation and BYOD usage to stop engineer burnout even when they’re not on call.
- SLO and metric comparison across teams, and how comparing team metrics rather than improving metrics such as DORA over time for a single team breeds animosity and demoralises engineers.
- Code reviews with jerkish or unhelpful comments, and the difference between radical candour through constructive feedback and pulling people down.
- Tool overload, and how selecting a common toolbox reduces the need for context switching.
- Flaky or poor testing, and how it builds mistrust and apathy in platform quality.
- Constant work items and a lack of learning time, and how a lack of training opportunities and space to grow leaves engineers feeling stuck.
- Lack of support for conference attendance and speaking, and how community connections help engineers grow and learn.

speaker: Andrew Poole
title: How to fall in love with automated tests!
description:
This session is in two parts:
1) How to get the maximum mileage from a minimal number of tests - end-to-end component tests
2) Integration Tests - how to not hate them and also sort out your local dev experience!

Part 1 Introduces, explains and demonstrates an approach to automated testing which covers as much of the surface area of your codebase as possible.

Imagine a unit test where the 'unit' is actually multiple executables! A single test can cover the whole happy path flow of a complex piece of orchestration, from API handlers, service bus handlers, database calls etc all in-memory, fast and with a nice fluent developer experience!

Because everything including the Program.cs and startup code are covered we can spot configuration and IoC issues which are hard to test with more traditional methods. I include a method of mocking and asserting against Azure Service Bus

Part 2 discusses the usual issues with integration tests and how they expose the issues with running an app locally. It shows some strategies for fixing some of those issues and actually making integration tests useful, mainly leaving the thing you are testing in a running state on your machine. This is a achieved by means of a script to set up local configuration without having to remember not to check env secrets into appsettings.dev files. Also using Fixtures which do things like setting up queues, topics and subscriptions.

The aim of both parts of this talk is to have a repo which when pulled down onto a fresh machine, builds first time, component tests pass first time, then having run the script and the app, the the integration tests pass first time, after which you can push F5 and have it all run with almost no time or effort!

speaker: Rachel Breeze
title: Rethinking Website Carbon Calculators: Alternative Ways to Measure Digital Emissions

speakerTaglines.rachel-breeze: Back End Development Team Lead, Umbraco and .NET Developer at Nexer Digital

description:
Website carbon calculators are widely used for estimating the environmental impact of websites. While they’re a helpful starting point, they often rely on general assumptions and incomplete data, which can lead to oversimplified or inaccurate results. Are they really telling the full story?

In this talk, we’ll take a closer look at the limitations of these tools—such as their reliance on averages for energy usage, lack of context about server efficiency, and ignoring how users actually interact with sites.  We’ll explore practical alternatives and ways of reducing your website's carbon footprint.

speaker: Dylan Beattie
title: How To Be A Rockstar Developer
description:
One evening in 2018, Dylan Beattie sat down in a bar, opened a laptop, and wrote a joke: a parody specification for Rockstar, a programming language based on the lyrics to 1980s power ballads. The joke was supposed to end there: a single Markdown file that folks would read, maybe laugh a bit, and then get on with their lives... well, that's not quite how it worked out. The internet's a big place, and a little corner of it  took Rockstar to their hearts: they found it, they loved it - and then they implemented it. Six years on, Rockstar has shown up  in the most unlikely places, from Classic Rock magazine, to Advent of Code, to Carnegie Mellon University and MIT - and each time, it attracts a new wave of aspiring Rockstar developers, with questions about how it works, and suggestions about how to make it better. And so, one evening in 2024, Dylan sat down in another bar, opened another laptop, and wrote another joke: "Rockstar 2.0: The Difficult Second Album".

On one level, Rockstar in 2024 is a stupid joke language based on Bon Jovi songs. On another level, it's packed with things that would have been impossible even just a few years ago: a project that combines .NET, C#, JavaScript, browser APIs, and web assembly, building on decades of research in parser engineering and asynchronous application development. And yes, it's still based on Bon Jovi songs.

This is the story of Rockstar 2.0. You'll learn about the history of esoteric programming languages, from INTERCAL, to Piet, to the researcher who taught Perl to speak Latin. You'll learn what's involved in creating an entirely new programming language. You'll see a lot of cool tech, you'll marvel at just how much engineering can go into one joke, and who knows - you might even qualify as a Certified Rockstar 2.0 Developer.

speaker: Stu Lang
title: Mutation Testing - Kill them mutants
description: A talk about Mutation Testing and Stryker

speaker: Vijay Patel
title: Rapid Prototypes & Throwaway Code
description:
Users don't always tell you what they really need.
And whiteboard sketches don't always make sense to everyone.
Rapid Prototypes help to get everyone on the same page,
And to find answers to complicated problems.

I'll walk through a real-life scenario in the world of "Drug Testing In The Olympics".

The talk will explain a real operational problem, describe what the Users wanted, and how we discovered what they *really needed*.

We'll use diagrams, UML and C# code to explore as we go.

This technique is inspired by "Model Exploration Whirlpool" in the Domain Driven Design community (the other DDD!).

speaker: Sean Farmar
title: Understanding The Business Problem
description:
One pattern I see again and again in software projects is related to the interaction between the business and the developers.

There are a few aspects to this, but one of the challenging ones is focusing on the solution instead of the problem the business is trying to solve, and this is done by both the business and the developers.

Another aspect is how well we, as developers, understand the business domain, mostly if we want to engage in Domain Driven Design.

In this talk, I will try to explain why it is so important to understand the business domain and the business problem we are trying to solve.

speaker: Kevlin Henney
title: Adventures in Spacetime
description:
Developers often find themselves caught in the crossfire of web calls, databases, microservices and other remote interactions. In battling all the infrastructure, platforms, middleware and frameworks their architecture has amassed, plus the legacy of code they may have inherited, they often don't have the chance to take a step back and consider the fundamental nature of distributed systems — fundamentals that limit what is possible and shape everything from the user experience to the breadth of architecture and the detail of code.

This is not a talk about APIs, SDKs, middleware or specific architectural styles, but a view of the fundamentals from the perspective of history, physics, code and entertainment. This talk takes in causality, clocks, relativity, CAP theorem, the fallacies of distributed computing and more!

speaker: Clifford Agius
title: Could a Co-Pilot be an Aircraft Co-Pilot
description:
Welcome aboard, fellow travelers!

In this talk, we’re strapping on our metaphorical aviator goggles and diving into the cockpit to explore the fascinating world of AI Co-Pilots and could they and more importantly should they be used in a real world flight deck?

Buckle up, because this flight is about to get bumpy—in a purely intellectual turbulence kind of way.

Using aircraft incidents and accidents we will see if an AI Co-Pilot would have saved the day... If you have a fear of flying maybe skip this one but I will say before you run out that none of the accidents are fatal so nothing to be scared of....

You don't need to be an AI specialist or even know anything about it, as we are just exploring the decisions pilots have to make in very limited timescales with limited information and throwing in some human factors to spice it up a bit. These are all good skills you can use in any decision making at work.

The aim of this session is to hopefully show you that AI can help but should we use it?

You will walk away knowing a bit about AI and have some fun geeking out on aviation.

speaker: Gary Ewan Park
title: Let's ship this thing!
description:
Have you ever been really excited about shipping a new version of your application, only to find out that you haven't done some of the administration "stuff" for it?

For example, understanding and documenting exactly what is included in the new release? Creating release notes for the end user, or even knowing what the "correct" next version number for the application should be!

In this session, we will look at a series of different strategies, and tools, that can be used to aid in the complete application development and deployment lifecycle, in order to allow you to "just ship it"!

speaker: Lotte Pitcher
title: Successfully Navigating Open Source Waters

speakerTaglines.lotte-pitcher: Microsoft MVP | Developer Advocate at Umbraco

description:
Diving into the open source world - whether as a consumer, contributor, or maintainer - can feel like navigating uncharted waters. How do you choose the right projects? What are the unspoken rules of engagement? How can you contribute effectively and build meaningful connections?

In this session we’ll go beyond the code to explore essential topics like licensing, governance, community dynamics and collaboration best practices.  We’ll review some popular open source projects to find inspiration in their successes and learn lessons from their challenges.

With over ten years of community contributions to the open source .NET CMS Umbraco, and now as a member of their Developer Relations team - Lotte knows the challenges of building a commercially viable product and a sustainable community, while still giving code away for free. Whether you’re a maintainer or a user of open source software, you’ll leave this session with actionable ideas on how to better navigate the open source waters -  because there’s much more to it than just “dotnet add package”!
